text:
ada (Infra): Heads up — we saw a partial outage in eu-west-2 affecting a subset of GPU pools starting ~10:32 UTC. We flipped weighted DNS to route traffic to eu-west-1 per the failover policy but some customers still hit eu-west-2. dns-bot posted health alerts.

DNS-bot: [ALERT] healthcheck failed for svc-inference.eu-west-2.redwood.internal -> 10/10 failed. Failover policy applied: weight eu-west-2=0, eu-west-1=100.

mike (SRE): Did we lower the authoritative TTL before flipping weights? If caches still had the old IPs they would keep going to eu-west-2.

ada (Ada typo?) — no, it's ada: I checked the zone — TTL is still 3600s for the A records. We normally set 60s for planned maintenance but this was an unexpected incident. Here's what `dig` returned a minute ago:

```
; <<>> DiG 9.16.1-Ubuntu <<>> svc-inference.eu-west-2.redwood.internal
;; ANSWER SECTION:
svc-inference.eu-west-2.redwood.internal. 3600 IN A 10.34.55.12
```

sophia (Neteng): Oof — 3600 explains it. Many recursive resolvers will honor that and keep talking to the old IP until TTL expires. Also note some public DNS caches (esp ISP caches and CDNs) have minimum caching or ignore very short TTLs. Changing the authoritative TTL now doesn't retroactively flush caches — it only affects future answers once the current TTL expires.

mike (SRE): So the root cause for the extended impact was TTL propagation + healthchecks not being picked up by some resolvers. What did the healthchecks look like at the LB/anycast level?

ada (Infra): Load balancer healthchecks were failing and we withdrew backend targets, but DNS-level weights still returned eu-west-2 for a bunch of clients due to caching. We also saw some customers using their own pinned IPs in env vars — those are expected to break.

leo (ProdEng): For clarity — the failover flow we used was: automatic health -> route53 weighted change (weight->0) -> infra console shows eu-west-1 taking traffic. That works for new lookups, but existing cached entries stayed on eu-west-2.

sophia (Neteng): Tactical notes for this incident:
- For unplanned failures, prefer control-plane routing shifts (BGP/anycast or LB-level failover) that don't rely on DNS cache expiry where possible.
- If DNS must be used, try to have the authoritative TTL short (<=60s) for production CNAMEs/ALIAS of services that need fast failover.
- If TTL is long, consider announcing a temporary fronting IP (anycast) or using the load balancer to rewrite traffic.

mike (SRE): We should capture the exact propagation observed. I pulled the query logs and saw resolvers with remaining TTL hitting eu-west-2 up to ~30 minutes after the change. That matches a 3600s record that had ~1800s remaining when we flipped.

ada (Infra): Action we did during incident:
1) Manually removed eu-west-2 backend targets from LBs (fast).
2) Updated DNS weights to 0 for eu-west-2 (immediate in authoritative zone).
3) Posted a note to customers recommending app-level DNS caching flush or restart if they had pinned IPs.

mike (SRE): Followups we need:
- Runbook update: Lower authoritative TTL to 60s for critical svc-records by default, with exception process for cost reasons.
- Add a pre-failover TTL change step for any planned migration (24h window recommended).
- Add monitoring that shows resolver-level distribution of answers (so we can measure propagation).

leo (ProdEng): Also add a step: if we foresee an outage, trigger LB-level failover first and DNS second. DNS is best-effort for drift only.

sophia (Neteng): Technical nuance: some global resolvers (e.g., Google Public DNS) will respect TTL but others may have minimums; negative caching or 301/302 redirects from intermediate caches can also cause surprises. We should avoid publishing glue records or registrar-level IPs for low-latency failover — keep the front door as an FQDN behind managed LB/anycast.

ada (Infra): Proposed immediate config change: set svc-inference.* authoritative TTL to 60s in all zones. We also need a postmortem doc entry outlining why we didn't anticipate the TTL problem.

mike (SRE): Agreed. Also add an ops play: when flipping DNS due to emergency, capture a sampling of resolvers (8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1, common ISP resolvers) and log their answers — helps quantify residual traffic.

ada (Infra): I'll open the runbook PR after the incident call. Action items: ada -> change TTL to 60s (now), mike -> add propagation monitoring query example to runbook, sophia -> draft note about resolver caveats, leo -> customer comms template for pinned-IP cases.

dns-bot: [INFO] zone change submitted: svc-inference.* TTL set to 60s. Change ID abc123.

mike (SRE): Quick example to include in runbook for checking propagation:
```
for r in 8.8.8.8 1.1.1.1; do dig @${r} svc-inference.redwood.internal +short +time=2; done
```
Point is to sample multiple resolvers, not just dig from prod.

ada (Infra): Post-incident notes: we still saw residual hits to eu-west-2 for ~25 minutes, but LB-level target removal prevented most traffic from hitting bad nodes. Customers with pinned IPs reported partial failures — follow-up outreach assigned to leo.

sophia (Neteng): Long-term: evaluate making critical service records managed by a DNS provider that supports instant failover routing + health checks at the DNS level (some providers support health-aware routing that reduces reliance on low TTLs). Also document registrar/GLUE implications.

mike (SRE): +1. Add a postmortem section: "DNS caching extended impact" with timeline and TTL numbers.

ada (Infra): Copying actions into the incident ticket now. Will follow up with PR and runbook changes. :thumbsup:

leo (ProdEng): Thanks all — good catch. We'll follow up with customers and the runbook updates. :eyes:
